subject: Chemistry
title: Why Is CH3Cl a Gas but CH3I a Liquid? Physical Properties of Haloalkanes
summary: Every trend follows from two things: the polar C–X bond (dipole–dipole attraction) and molecular size / mass (van der Waals forces). In this lesson: why boiling points are higher than the parent alkanes (dipole–dipole and van der Waals forces), R–I ＞ R–Br ＞ R–Cl ＞ R–F against the room-temperature line, branching lowers the boiling point, para-dichlorobenzene melts highest, density and why haloalkanes barely dissolve in water. Two ordering questions solved.

notes.title: Why Is CH3Cl a Gas but CH3I a Liquid? Physical Properties of Haloalkanes
notes.blurb: boiling points, melting points of dihalobenzenes, density and solubility, solved questions

keyPoints: **Higher b.p.**: Haloalkanes boil **above** their parent alkanes. Polar C–X and **more mass**.
**Halogen order**: Bigger halogen → **stronger** attractions. CH₃I liquid, CH₃Cl **gas** at 25 °C.
**Dihalobenzenes**: Symmetry → better **crystal packing**. p-C₆H₄Cl₂ melts at **323 K**.

blocks.p: Haloalkanes boil higher than their parent hydrocarbons (e.g. CH₄ −162 °C, CH₃Cl −24 °C): the C–X bond is polar (dipole–dipole forces) and the mass is greater (stronger van der Waals forces).

head: Trend
Example
rows: Same alkyl group: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F

blocks.p: Branched molecules are more spherical, so the area of contact (and the van der Waals attraction) is smaller.

o-, m- and p-dichlorobenzene boil at nearly the same temperature (453, 446, 448 K), but the **para** isomer melts much higher (323 K vs 256 K and 249 K): it is symmetrical and fits the crystal lattice better.

list: ✗ Branching raises the b.p. (it lowers it).
✗ Para isomer has the highest b.p. (it has the highest m.p.; the b.p. values are nearly equal).
✗ Haloalkanes dissolve in water because they are polar.

blocks.p: **Q1.** Increasing b.p.: CH₃Cl (−24 °C) < CH₃Br (4 °C) < CH₂Br₂ (97 °C) < CHBr₃ (149 °C): size and mass increase.
**Q2.** Increasing b.p.: isopropyl chloride (36 °C, branched) < 1-chloropropane (47 °C) < 1-chlorobutane (78 °C, longer chain).
